by_area.notes: Counted in semesters, not credits. Eight semesters (Class of 2029+ and Classes of 2027-28).
Six semesters (both). Class of 2029+: one semester must be Civics.
Six semesters (both). Class of 2029+: one semester must be Financial Literacy.
Three semesters (two if student athlete; PE Teacher and Coach Agreement must be completed).

by_area.area: Visual Arts / Music or Performing Arts / Career and/or Technical Education, Design, and Engineering
by_area.notes: Six semesters in a combination of these areas. Class of 2029+: one semester must be Career Exploration.
Class of 2029+: six semesters; Classes of 2027-28: two semesters. Can be additional semesters in any area above once minimums are met; includes world language.

other: Requirements are stated in semesters; a semester is a single-block semester-long course, and courses that meet for 2 blocks count as two semesters.
Class of 2029 and beyond: one Global Citizenship semester must be Civics; one Mathematics semester must be Financial Literacy; one semester in the arts/CTE group must be Career Exploration.
A one-period, one-semester course may only fulfill one content area per semester although there may be a choice of content area.
Equivalent learning opportunities (internships, work-based learning, independent study) leading to documented proficiency may substitute for traditional courses.
Completion of a Senior Capstone Project (yearlong; waived for seniors in Vermont's Early College Program).
Demonstrated performance in Areas of Personal Proficiency (Lead, Express, Solve, Connect, Care, Achieve) via a MAP (Meaningful Academic Plan).
Minimum grade to earn course credit is 2.0 (4 point scale).
graduation_requirements.raw_text: To that end, graduation from Danville High School is based on three benchmarks: Courses (Class of 2029 and beyond) Eight semesters of English/Language Arts Six semesters of Global Citizenship *One Semester must be Civics Six semesters of Mathematics *One Semester must be Financial Literacy Six semesters of Science Three semesters of Physical Education *Two semester if student athlete (PE Teacher and Coach Agreement must be completed) One semester of Health Six semesters of a combination of the following course areas, based on postsecondary path and student interest: Visual Arts Music or Performing Arts Career and/or Technical Education, Design, and Engineering *One Semester must be Career Exploration Six semesters of Electives - This can be additional semesters in any area above, once the minimum requirements are met, and includes world language. Courses (Class of 2027 and 2028) Eight semesters of English/Language Arts Six semesters of Global Citizenship Six semesters of Mathematics Six semesters of Science Three semesters of Physical Education *Two semester if student athlete (PE Teacher and Coach Agreement must be completed) One semester of Health Six semesters of a combination of the following course areas, based on postsecondary path and student interest: Visual Arts Music or Performing Arts Career and/or Technical Education, Design, and Engineering Two semesters of Electives - This can be additional semesters in any area above, once the minimum requirements are met, and includes world language. Some courses are interdisciplinary in nature and offer semester credit in more than one content area. A one-period, one-semester course may only fulfill one content area per semester although there may be a choice of content area. Equivalent learning opportunities, including internships, work-based learning or independent study leading to documented proficiency in the above areas may substitute for traditional semester or year long courses. Danville School encourages students to advocate for themselves and their learning goals, and will be advised by our Pathways coordinator and school counselor. Students are strongly encouraged to take courses above and beyond these minimum requirements. Excessive downtime during the high school day does not reflect well in the eyes of future colleges, employers or other post-secondary institutions. *A semester, for the purpose of documenting coursework, is defined as a single-block semester-long course. Courses that meet for 2 blocks will count as two semesters. Each teacher shares their grading criteria through their syllabus at the start of the course. Grades are reported on a 4 point scale. The minimum grade to earn course credit at Danville is 2.0. Completion of a Senior Capstone Project A yearlong endeavor that includes project development, community service, inquiry, new learning, oral presentation and a written essay. Information on the Senior Project can be found in the Senior Capstone Project Handbook * In accordance with state law, this requirement is waived for seniors participating in Vermont’s Early College Program. Demonstrated Performance in Areas of Personal Proficiency Students will demonstrate proficiency in Vermont’s transferable skills in classes, but also through a MAP (personal learning plan called the Meaningful Academic Plan) built throughout their high school career.

courses.description: In this course, we will shift our focus from the numbers to reasoning about the operations on those numbers. In doing so, we set the stage for higher level mathematics. We will practice the algebraic habits of mind: seek and use structure, use tools strategically, puzzle and persevere, describe repeated reasoning and communicate with precision. Topics will include: distributive property, linear equations, inequalities, functions, systems of equations, graphing, factoring polynomials, quadratics, exponents, and word problems and mathematical language.

This is the standard entry level math course required for all students. Two formats are available, full year and single semester, so that students can move at their own pace. Algebra I provides a formal development of the algebraic skills and concepts necessary for students to succeed in advanced courses. The concept of function is emphasized throughout the course. Topics include: operations with real numbers, linear equations and inequalities, relations and functions, polynomials, algebraic fractions, and nonlinear equations. Proficiency with Algebraic concepts will be necessary for success in all other high school math courses. The successful student in Algebra I will move on to Geometry or Algebra II.
courses.notes: Two formats available: full year and single semester.

courses.description: This course studies the properties and applications of geometric figures in 2 and 3 dimensions. Algebra 1 skills will be utilized throughout the course. This course is designed to emphasize the study of the properties and applications of common geometric figures in two and three dimensions. It includes the study of transformations and right triangle trigonometry. Inductive and deductive thinking skills are used in problem solving situations, and applications to the real world are stressed. It also emphasizes writing proofs to solve (prove) properties of geometric figures. Students that successfully complete this course should take Algebra 2 (unless they have already completed Algebra 2, in which case they would move on to Pre-Calculus or Statistics).

Algebra 2 builds upon the concepts learned in Algebra 1 and Geometry (although it is possible to take Algebra 2 prior to, or concurrent with Geometry). This course is an extension of Algebra I and provides further development of the concept of a function. Topics include: relations, functions, equations and inequalities, polynomials, algebraic fractions, logarithmic and exponential functions, sequences and series; and counting principles and probability. Students who successfully complete Algebra II will move on to Pre-Calculus and/or Statistics.

Workplace Math is designed to be an option for students looking to take a math course their junior or senior year who are more interested in the trades and not necessarily college bound. The curriculum is flexible and can be molded to fit the needs, abilities and interests of the students in the class. Measurement and estimation, along with design and building will play a major role in the course. Other possible topics could include marketing, client communication (i.e. figuring the details of commissioned work and producing a reasonable quote.) Most of the work for this course will be done in the classroom so students need to come to class with a working mindset.

In this introductory finance course, students learn best practices for managing their own finances. Students learn skills in creating budgets, developing long-­term financial plans to meet their goals, and making responsible choices about income and expenses. Students will explore concepts such as saving and investing, loans and credit scores. This course also includes an overview of personal income taxes and organizing annual information. Students are inspired by experiences of finance professionals and stories of everyday people and the choices they make to manage their money.
courses.fulfills_text: Graduation Requirement - Class of 2029 and beyond
courses.notes: Graduation requirement heading: "Graduation Requirement - Class of 2029 and beyond"; one of the six semesters of Mathematics must be Financial Literacy.

courses.description: This course will prepare students for entry into college-level mathematics by developing personal discipline and abstract problem solving skills while delving into the world of Precalculus. Students will practice complex algebraic and graphical reasoning in the first semester. In the second semester, students will relate this to upper level trigonometry and periodic functions. The course will end with students engaging in an introduction to Calculus concepts, such as limits and derivatives. For students interested in further studies in mathematics or science fields, this course is a must.

This course offers college credit through Southern New Hampshire University (SNHU) Calculus is a field of math devoted to analyzing how things change, numerically, algebraically and graphically. Students will learn to describe various situations by applying functions and investigating their characteristics, especially in business, economics, physical and biological sciences. Students interested in math, science, or economic fields should take this course as a preliminary to college math studies.

This course offers college credit through Southern New Hampshire University (SNHU) Statistics is the study, collection and interpretation of data. Why do airlines overbook flights? Is there a relationship between IQ scores and study habits? How can you analyze the overall performance of a pitcher? Many varied fields of study use statistics to represent data and communicate effectively. This course asks students to analyze the big picture situation while using math, calculators and computer programs to support their interpretation in descriptive writing.

This survey course will prepare students for their high school English courses. Students will perfect their essay writing, master their grammar, and hone their reading skills. This course will feature texts from a variety of genres and time periods with a focus on Vermont and American Literature. Students in this course should expect periodic homework assignments, occasional research projects, and frequent class discussions.
courses.fulfills_text: Required for all ninth grade students.

courses.description: This world literature-focused literature and writing class will build on the skills introduced in English 9. Students will explore a variety of world cultures through the lens of literature and practice argumentative, research, and creative writing. Reading will consist of a variety of full-group and choice books. Small and large group discussion, as well as reading and writing assignments, are a required and substantial part of class.

Students will read a variety of short stories or novellas that each stand on their own as a work of artistic expression. After analyzing elements of the text, students watch the movie version and analyze how each art form works to tell a compelling story. Students discuss narrative elements such as character, plot, setting, dialogue, tension, endings, foreshadowing, and writer/director’s purpose. Students will develop their reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills as they analyze both the literary text and the film. Students will develop media literacy skills as they examine how films can shape societal attitudes or reflect upon the cultural moment in which they are made. Objective: students will be able to communicate effectively in discussion and in writing as they show their understanding of literary and cinematic elements.

In this intermediate writing class, students will study the craft of writing through personal and creative expression. We will practice composition and revision techniques by writing fiction, poetry, plays, creative nonfiction, and analytical essays. Students will workshop material with peers, read independently and in class, and learn the basics of literary analysis. By the end of the semester, students will produce a collection of creative and academic writing and have an opportunity to publish their work in a school anthology.
courses.notes: Description refers to "the end of the semester".

courses.description: This course will give students the opportunity to develop stories into screenplays. Over the course of the semester, we’ll examine a number of Hollywood scripts to discuss elements such as pacing, character development, dialogue, and tone; we’ll try to apply the lessons we learn from these master works to our own stories. Students will learn how to write in industry standard format so that their work is ready to pitch to movie makers. Writing exercises will be numerous and students will develop a short film screenplay for their final project.
courses.notes: Description refers to "the course of the semester".

courses.description: Students read books and articles about inventions and innovations and understand the interplay between science and literature. Students read three non-fiction books about young people engaged in life-changing inventions and read short works about innovations and inventions. Students will also explore their own interests in invention and innovation. This will be both an investigative and analytical class. Some of the essential questions we will address are: What inventions are the most important ones in our lives today? What inventions were critical in their time but have been replaced by greater inventions? Are inventions always good? What inventions have dangerous (seen/unforeseen) consequences? Who gets credit for their inventions and who gets left out and why? How will AI shape your life?

No matter what your plans after high school, it’s imperative that you know how to communicate. This advanced writing class will build on student’s writing skills and practices to encourage more nuanced, persuasive, and concise written expression. This course will cover a range of writing styles to help students gain flexibility and confidence with the written word. Students will read and examine a variety of non-fiction forms and students will write and revise their own essays. This class will also prepare students for more advanced college writing courses.
courses.prerequisites: Two years of English, or instructor’s approval.

courses.description: This is an outdoor-classroom based class. It’s an experiential learning class where students spend all or part of their class time outside, writing and learning about their place in the natural world. Class meets in the yurt outside. From the yurt, we take walks to observe our natural surroundings and write about our observations. Students read excerpts from a variety of nature writers’ work and respond to those writers’ ideas as well as develop their own writing through journaling. Experiential learning is a key component of this class. This class builds students’ sense of place, helps students develop scientific inquiry and investigation skills, encourages students to be collaborative and builds community. This course strengthens students’ transferable thinking skills and connects students with nature in creative ways.

Often we forget that there is an entire world beyond the border of Vermont, or even the United States. The two semester sequence of World Geography/World History provides students with an in-depth look at the development of places around the world and sets the foundation for better understanding of United States and Global History. In addition, the study of geography will play an important role as students study the development of regional cultures, political and economic systems, environmental issues, and the history of regions across the globe. Knowledge about the world beyond the United States is important to be an active and responsible global citizen in order to make informed decisions and help recognize the interconnectedness between people and our environment. First Semester: Cultural exploration of the main regions of the world: North America, Latin America, Europe, Russia, Middle East, Africa and Asia Second Semester: The Enlightenment until World War II. Includes the Renaissance and the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, modern development of African and Asian Nations, the rise of Imperialism,
courses.notes: Described as a two semester sequence (First Semester / Second Semester) with World History.

courses.description: This is an introductory course to the power of public speaking, oration, and words. Emphasis will be in improving your public speaking and argument skills through organization and delivery, control and enunciation. Listening and analytic skills will be also be stressed throughout the course. Students will also develop an awareness of the consequences of communication and acquire an appreciation of the responsibilities of ethical communication.

In this course, students will begin with a review and analysis of the American Constitution, then move on to Industrialization and the forming of modern America. The course will also examine America's role in various global conflicts. Inquiries and content will extend to America’s development at home and America's role in the world, tracing the social, economic, political, geographic and cultural forces that have shaped the history of the United States to the present day. Emphasizes understanding of contemporary issues in light of our past.

courses.course_name: History of Women in the United States
courses.description: What role did women play in key events in American History? What were women’s lives like before the arrival of European settlers, during the colonial period, during World War II, during the 19th and 20th centuries? What was it like to be accused of Witchcraft or to be a slave on a plantation? Why did the feminist movement take off in the 1960s? In this course you will enhance your knowledge of women’s roles throughout American history by reading first-hand accounts from the women who lived during these and many other U.S. historical events. Semester 1: 1600-1900 (course A) Semester 2: 1900 to present day (course B)
courses.notes: Semester 1: 1600-1900 (course A); Semester 2: 1900 to present day (course B).

courses.description: The purpose of this government course is to provide students with a background in the philosophy, functions, and structure of the United States government. Students will examine the philosophical foundations of the United States government and how that philosophy developed. Students will also examine the structure and function of the United States government including the purpose and operation of the branches of government under the Constitution and how it has evolved through time and its relationship to states and citizens. Students will look at current events through the scope of modern day government and human rights.
courses.fulfills_text: One Semester must be Civics (Class of 2029 and beyond)

courses.course_name: CCV Ethnicity and Diversity in the USA
courses.description: This course explores aspects of ethnic, regional, racial, religious, and economic diversity as they influence contemporary United States society and culture. Students will examine different assumptions and attitudes about diversity and 'multiculturalism' and examine the changing demographics of the United States population. Students will analyze the homogenizing and divisive influences of media, education, the workplace, and the political process; analyze how media, education, workplace, and the political process reinforce diversity as a social and cultural reality; compare theories of social stratification and resulting inequalities among different ethnic, race, class, and religious groups.

Often we forget that there is an entire world beyond the border of Vermont, or even the United States. The two-semester sequence of Cultural Geography/World History provides students with an in-depth look at the development of places around the world and sets the foundation for better understanding of the United States and Global History. In addition, the study of geography will play an important role as students study the development of regional cultures, political and economic systems, environmental issues, and the history of regions across the globe. Knowledge about the world beyond the United States is important to be an active and responsible global citizen in order to make informed decisions and help recognize the interconnectedness between people and our environment.
courses.notes: Described as a two-semester sequence with Cultural Geography.

courses.description: This course examines contemporary problems in a global context such as poverty, social inequality, crime, religious and ethnic conflict, resource availability, population pressure and the spread of infectious diseases. Attention will be given to the current state of social institutions and the nature of social change while exploring how social problems are defined and perceived by various groups as matters of public and global concern. This course will integrate many social themes and will critically analyze attempts to resolve problems using the methodologies of social science and a range of theoretical perspectives.

Intro to psychology provides students with a foundational understanding of the major components of the field of psychology - including traditional and historical approaches, major theories, brain function, and research methodology. The course will allow students to explore topics of personal relevance such as self-esteem, the meaning of dreams, personality theory, addiction, childhood development, and more. By actively participating in social experiments and research, students will gain first-hand insight into how psychology affects their everyday lives. This course earns CCV college credit.
courses.prerequisites: World History or equivalent, two additional semesters of global citizenship coursework

courses.description: A survey of the basic issues, concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Students learn to think critically about the nature of society and social institutions, and the relationship among individuals and groups. Topics will include social organization, socialization and social change, social stratification, class and class conflict, gender, race, and ethnicity. Students will differentiate between functionalist, conflict, and interactionist explanations of deviance and social control; compare theories of social stratification and discuss resulting inequalities such as class, power, prestige, gender, ethnicity, age, and ability; demonstrate and interpret how demographic and statistical research is used to understand and respond to social change and recognize critical questions about quantitative claims. This course earns CCV college credit.
courses.prerequisites: World History or equivalent, two additional semesters of global citizenship coursework

courses.description: Forensics and Criminal Justice is a course that dives into the fascinating realm of crime and punishment, and the science used to help inform these systems. Students enrolled in this course will learn about how our society deals with criminals and their victims through the legal and social processes that exist within the United States. They’ll participate in a mock trial to help them better understand the responsibilities of trial lawyers and mock crime scene investigations to help them better understand the work dedicated forensic scientists conduct in the name of justice.

like to pursue. With guidance from the independent learning advisors, they will choose content or Danville’s Areas of Personal Proficiency, identify learning goals and products, and map out a schedule for their semester. Their work will be assessed by a panel of teachers throughout the semester, and they will receive coaching and attend seminars with the independent learning advisors.
courses.prerequisites: Generally available for 10th grade and above, based on approval by Personalized Learning Advisors.

courses.description: Prerequisites: To be determined by content area teacher In the Guided Personal Study, students will work closely with a teacher who provides content for them to learn. This could be an online class, a class not offered that semester, or a specialized study discussed by the teacher and student. Students will gain the credit associated with the course of study they're pursuing.
courses.prerequisites: To be determined by content area teacher

courses.description: In this structured independent study, students will explore a career or careers of interest. They will conduct a personal inventory to be matched with potential careers, update their resume, learn about their rights as a 21st century worker, learn about different application processes, and research the preparation needed to prepare for a career or careers of their choice. Career explorations may include job shadows and/or some form of short term internship or internships. This independent study may be taken for English or Elective credit. Other types of credit may be available with special permission.
courses.prerequisites: Available to 10th graders and above with permission by Pathways Coordinator and School Counselor.
courses.fulfills_text: This independent study may be taken for English or Elective credit. Other types of credit may be available with special permission. (Class of 2029 and beyond: One Semester must be Career Exploration)

courses.description: Students will explore the fundamentals of entrepreneurship. They will develop skills in the practical aspects of communicating in the business world. Students have two options: 1. Planning their own business or; 2. Being a part of the school store management team Students will also seek out expertise from community partners and mentors. Occasional field trips and out-of-school workshops will be components of this Independent Study. Students can choose between Global Citizenship, English, or Elective credit.
courses.fulfills_text: Students can choose between Global Citizenship, English, or Elective credit.

courses.description: This course covers the basics of light construction, building code, field applications, and how regional culture and tradition influences techniques and standards. . Topics covered will include: masonry, welding, carpentry, mechanical, electrical and related fields. Content is based on the techniques of each trade and the interrelationships between them with a focus on home construction in the New England region. . Instruction will focus on the critical actions, knowledge, systems, and processes necessary to participate in a design/build enterprise. Activities will focus on tools and terminology, manufacturing processes and production, quality and continuous improvement practices, maintenance awareness, and safety. Students will develop high performance skills through demonstrations, lectures, a semester-long class building project, group work and evaluation, technical presentations, critical thinking exercises, and problem‐solving case studies. Students will learn to demonstrate the core set of skills and knowledge necessary to take the first step in preparing for sustained careers in today's high performance, fast paced environment.

Woodworking is an option for students to earn academic credit while using the shop, outdoors, and surrounding community as their classroom. This program emphasizes teamwork, leadership, professionalism, craftsmanship, career exploration and critical thinking. This is a program for all learners, especially students who might be considering attending a program at a regional technical center for their junior or senior years, and may be interested in a future career in the trades, or a technical field. We believe many students have skills and strengths that aren’t always recognized in the traditional classroom format, including group leadership, applied technical skills, and self-advocacy. It is not an “alternative” program, meaning students with all learning styles, whether or not they’ve found success in the traditional classroom are welcomed, and will be challenged.

Intro to Design and Fabrication is a hands-on, project-based course that introduces students to the fundamentals of design thinking, creative problem-solving, and fabrication processes. Students will explore how ideas move from concept to prototype through the use of digital design tools, computer-aided design (CAD), and shop fabrication techniques. Projects will integrate art, engineering, and technology, encouraging students to design, build, test, and refine their ideas. Students will learn how to use tools safely and effectively to bring their designs to life. Instruction emphasizes Design, collaboration, iteration, and reflection. Students will engage in individual and group projects. This course serves as an introduction to both Industrial Arts and Woodworking, preparing students for advanced coursework or technical programs in the trades.

Introductory Life Science students focus their studies on foundational concepts in biology. This course encourages students to think flexibly across disciplines and to use the practices of science and engineering to problem solve and explain phenomena in the world around them. Students will engage regularly in mathematical thinking, close reading of informational texts, evidence-based writing, and the communication of ideas to an audience of their peers. This cross-disciplinary curriculum aligns with the Performance Expectations of the Next Generation Science Standards which are designed to move students towards competency in science as it is practiced in the 21st century.
courses.notes: Titled "Introductory Life Science" in prerequisites of other courses.

courses.description: In Physical Science, students engage in a range of subjects including chemistry, physics, and engineering. This approach is designed to prepare students for the world today in which the greatest technological and scientific challenges require collaboration between traditionally distinct disciplines. From global warming to competition for limited resources, scientists and engineers from diverse backgrounds must work together to inform society’s decision making processes. As well as learning content from a variety of subjects, students in this course also practice skills drawn from multiple disciplines. They engage regularly in mathematical thinking, close reading of informational texts, evidence-based writing, and the communication of ideas to an audience of their peers. This cross-disciplinary curriculum aligns with the Performance Expectations of the Next Generation Science Standards which are designed to move students towards competency in science as it is practiced in the 21st century.

This is a hands-on course where students will learn the principles of ecology through designing and implementing field experiments that examine biological diversity and interactions, watershed and lake ecology, landscapes and their history, invasive species, and human impact. As a culminating project, students will create management plans for local terrestrial or aquatic communities, or a species of their choice. Students will be actively learning the tools of the trade, performing field research, and observing and collecting specimens from our local lakes and streams, town forests, rail trail, and school grounds to supplement their growing global perspective on factors influencing ecology. Topics studied will include carrying capacity, biodiversity, cycling of matter and energy flow, succession, behavior, and stability and change of ecosystems. As a part of their studies, students will be contributing to the development of a long-term database of species diversity in the local area.

Lake Ecology is a hands-on course focused on studying the major components of lake ecosystems ranging from biological diversity and interactions, to physical and chemical interactions, to the human impact on lake systems. Students will be actively performing field research and hands-on lab activities to explore the factors influencing lake ecology. Topics studied will include biodiversity and phenology, energy flow, water and heat budgets, watersheds, invasive species, lake stratification and turnover, and stability and change of lake ecosystems.

In this laboratory science course students investigate living systems from large to small scale with a focus on applications to daily life. This is a general biology course that includes mammalian cell structure and function, cellular reproduction and physiology, the central dogma of biology (DNA to proteins) and Mendelian genetics. The laboratory portion of this course will extend the understanding and application of concepts through hand-on exercises. Students engage in the practices of science including problem solving, critical thinking, and application of the scientific method through independent and collaborative work.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science and Introductory Life Science, and at least one intermediate course.

courses.description: products that are designed to help students succeed at complex, authentic challenges to construct a solid understanding of environmental science. This course not only engages the fundamentals of environmental science, but also shows students how science informs sustainability, environmental policies, economics and personal choice.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science and Introductory Life Science.

courses.description: Earth Science deals largely with the geologic materials, structure, and ever-changing systems (think tens of millions of years) on our planet. Topics will include rocks and minerals, plate tectonics, earthquakes, orogeny (mountain building), volcanoes, structural geology, and stratigraphic sections. Local to global scales will be considered. Students will learn to make observations of their surroundings and use a variety of tools to unravel previous events at a specific site. Be prepared to go outdoors in a variety of conditions.

Physics is a hand-on laboratory course focused on force, motion, matter and energy. This course has a strong emphasis on utilizing science and engineering practices. Students will create models to explore and elucidate physics concepts such as forces and their interactions, motion in one and two dimensions, nuclear processes, energy, wave properties and electromagnetic radiation. Virtual labs will be employed in addition to hands-on physical labs to help students fully explore and achieve a deeper understanding of the concepts under investigation.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science and Introductory Life Science, Algebra 2 or concurrent
courses.notes: 4 College credits earned through CCV (3 course + 1 Lab)

courses.description: Chemistry is a hand-on laboratory course investigating the properties and interactions of matter. This course has a strong focus on science and engineering practices and students will create and utilize models ranging from small to large scale to elucidate and explore chemistry concepts. Both hands-on physical labs, as well as virtual labs, will be used to probe and solidify understanding of topics including atomic structure, periodicity, properties of matter, chemical reactions, solutions, chemical bonding, stoichiometry, energy and an introduction to organic chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Physical Science and Introductory Life Science
courses.notes: 4 college credits earned through CCV. (3 course + 1 lab)

courses.description: Renewable Energy Systems provides introductory instruction and hands-on experience with energy transformations. Solar, wind, and hydropower electric systems will be used to learn about capturing, storing, and manipulating electrical energy. Heat generation, efficiency, and conservation concepts will be studied through the lense of model efficient home experiments. Additionally, our current and widely used non-renewable energy sources will be assessed.

Students refine their skills on their instruments in a large ensemble and small ensemble setting. Band meets Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. Students enhance their technical skills through their studies in band literature. Students are placed in small groups for weekly lessons and small ensemble work, and have the opportunity to perform in various concerts throughout the year, including Cafe Night. Festivals: Northeast District, VT All-State, and New England.

Students study a variety of vocal works, including movie music, the pops, show tunes, and the classics. Chorus meets Tuesdays and Thursdays. Students study vocal technique through performance practice, both in the full chorus and in special groups. Students have the opportunity to perform in various concerts throughout the year, including Cafe Night. Festivals: Northeast District, VT All-State, New England.
Students will learn high level technical skills while working in a small ensemble. Students are expected to take at least one audition and perform in a special concert.
courses.prerequisites: Open to advanced instrumentalists and/or vocalists in grades 11 & 12, by permission from the teacher. May include an audition.

courses.description: In Piano Lab, students will learn the fundamentals of playing the piano. Students of all experience levels are welcome. Curriculum will form itself around the experience of each student. Units may include: chords, melodies, patterns, technique, rock history, songwriting, musical genres, and current topics in music. Students are not required to perform in concerts, but it is an option for all who are interested.

Music Lab is a crash-course in all things music, and it can be tailored to the interests of each student. Units may include: rock history, songwriting and analysis, musical genres, significant musical performances, and current topics in music. Curriculum will form itself around the experience of each student. Students are not required to perform in concerts, but it is an option for all who are interested. Want to learn a new instrument? Want to propose an independent project? This class is for you.

The Guitar Lab course is split into two semesters. Fall (String I) is a beginning level course, and spring (String II) is intended for those who have taken String I or who already have some string experience. Students will learn the basics of playing acoustic guitar and related instruments, including ukulele and bass. We will explore the fundamentals of song structure with chord progressions, rhythm, bass lines and melodies. Students will read and create tablature and chord charts, and techniques will include strumming, fingerpicking, and improvising within a scale. There will be both informal and formal performance opportunities for students to share their learning with classmates and others in the community.
courses.notes: Split into two semesters: Fall (String I) beginning level; spring (String II) for those who have taken String I or have some string experience.

courses.description: In this introductory level course students will explore 2-dimensional art making techniques (drawing, painting, mixed media, printmaking, collage, etc.,) methods and media. Art history, both ancient and contemporary, will be taught using a variety of methods. Weekly sketchbook prompts, classroom projects, and a final project are among some of the assignments for this course. Intro to Drawing and Painting may be taken independently of Intro to Sculpture

In this introductory level course students will explore 3-dimensional art making techniques (paper mache, clay, recycled sculpture, plaster casting, environmental sculpture, etc.,) methods and media. Art history, both ancient and contemporary, will be taught using a variety of methods. Weekly sketchbook assignments, classroom projects, and a final project are among some of the assignments for this course. Intro to Drawing and Painting may be taken independently of Intro to Sculpture.

In this intermediate level course (prerequisite of Intro to Drawing and Painting) students will explore a variety of digital design methods including (but not limited to): digital photography with DSLR cameras and Adobe PhotoShop, digital layout with Adobe InDesign, digital illustration and drawing with Adobe Illustrator. Students will complete a range of projects including typography, product marketing, logo design, rebranding an existing organization, designing promotional materials, and more! In addition to digital art making methods students will learn about and create with serigraphy (silk screen printing), as well as traditional visual art media. Students will gain useful, real world skills in time management, marketing, teamwork, and design principles.
courses.notes: Intermediate level course (prerequisite of Intro to Drawing and Painting)

courses.description: In this intermediate level course, students will become well rounded in the fundamentals of digital photography. Four areas of instruction will be emphasized: How cameras work, how composition works, how lighting works, and how to use photo editing software. The history of photography and photographers is explored through reading assignments, presentations, guest visitors, field trips, and student research. Cameras will be provided for students during this course. Students are welcome to use a device of their own if they prefer (digital camera, or smartphone).

This intermediate level course explores both handbuilding and wheel clay techniques. Students learn the basic techniques of pinch, coil, and slab building, glazing, surface decoration, and working on the potter’s wheel. Proper and safe working methods while using hand tools, glazes and the kiln will be emphasized. The history of ceramics and an introduction to historic and contemporary ceramic artists will be discussed.

In this advanced level, SNHU college credit course, students continue to work with the fundamentals of drawing from observation and imagination in a variety of media. Students will learn and practice techniques for handling various media, and will explore artists from around the world. Elements of Art and Principles of Design will be studied and used in making two-dimensional works of art. Students will create a digital portfolio of their work, and will curate a student art exhibit at the end of the semester.
courses.prerequisites: Intro to Drawing and Painting, Photography or Ceramics; instructor approval
courses.notes: 3 college credits possible through SNHU; advanced level

courses.description: Students are introduced to elementary concepts and skills in Spanish. Listening, Writing, Reading and Speaking skills are practiced. This is a yearlong course. In exceptional cases students can join the course starting in the second semester. For example, students who join Danville School from other institutions in Spring Semester can take the class only for the language they already studied in the previous institution (French and/or Spanish). Students who wish to join mid-year must obtain instructor permission, and complete a series of preparatory assignments.
courses.fulfills_text: These courses meet the graduation requirements as elective courses: 1 credit/language/semester

courses.description: Students continue and deepen their exploration of concepts and skills in Spanish. Listening, Writing, Reading and Speaking skills are practiced.
courses.prerequisites: Spanish I at Danville School, or previous instruction for transfer students.
courses.fulfills_text: These courses meet the graduation requirements as elective courses: 1 credit/language/semester

courses.description: This class is for any student who needs a different/higher level curriculum in Spanish than the Introductory or Intermediate levels curricula can provide. Exploring Italian could also be an option. Advanced study will include a teaching internship, recognizing that teaching a subject is one of the best ways to consolidate one’s own learning.
courses.fulfills_text: These courses meet the graduation requirements as elective courses: 1 credit/language/semester

courses.description: Students who enroll in this course will be presented with developmentally appropriate material to address one’s overall wellness. Health topic areas to be covered include: Alcohol, Tobacco, and Other Drugs, Family, Social and Sexual Health, Mental and Emotional Health, Nutrition and Physical Activity, Personal Health and Wellness, and Violence and Injury Prevention. The course’s main focus is for students to address health related issues that may arise during their high school years and beyond.

The physical/recreational education program at Danville High School parallels the state standards for physical education. It is based on the disciplines of motor learning, biomechanics, exercise physiology, human growth and development, sociology, and historical perspectives. It stresses physical/recreational activities that help the student develop socially and emotionally as well as physically, through regular participation in physical activity. The student will realize the value of active involvement in the program while receiving instruction in sports and methods of maintaining fitness, which will have the potential to improve the quality of their adult life.

The Planning for Lifelong Fitness class is designed to provide each student with the knowledge needed to understand the importance of strength and fitness training and the knowledge of developing proper nutritional habits. Students will understand the importance of setting goals for personal improvement and achievement, and will leave the class with a lifelong understanding of how to maintain adequate physical fitness for a healthy lifestyle. All students will be provided with the necessary training on each specific exercise so that the exercise process can be safe and productive. Students are encouraged to remain positive with themselves, as well as with other students in order to maintain a good training atmosphere. It is important to realize that everyone begins this course, and progresses through this course at his/her own rate, as they reach their own individual goals. Safety is always given the first priority in this class. The TriFit Evaluation System and the use of heart rate monitors will be an important tool used in documenting the progress of each student.

courses.course_name: ASPIRE (Achieving Successful Pathways through Individualized Relevant Education)
courses.description: ASPIRE is a comprehensive life skills class designed to support students in developing practical skills and habits for daily living and future independence. Throughout the school year, students will engage in activities and lessons across four key areas: ● Community Living: Gain confidence and competence in navigating the school and local community, including transportation, safety, budgeting, and social participation. ● Domestic Living: Learn essential household skills, including cooking, cleaning, organization, and personal care, to foster independence at home. ● Leisure and Recreation: Discover and cultivate personal interests and hobbies, promoting individual fulfillment and positive social interactions. ● Vocational Training: Explore career pathways and develop job-ready skills through hands-on experiences, workplace simulations, and career preparation activities. Throughout the school year, students participate in a variety of activities designed to strengthen these areas, including: ● Following and discussing current news events ● Playing educational games to enhance problem-solving and social skills ●   Learning maps and geography ●   Practicing telling time, counting money, and budgeting ●   Developing personal care routines ●   Building social communication skills ●   Practicing reading and vocabulary development ●   Exploring cooking and understanding food groups Through ASPIRE, students will build the knowledge, skills, and confidence needed to thrive in their homes, communities, and future workplaces.
